title: How many targets and how often
summary: Starting points for a beginner: how many targets per session, how often to train and why the quality of each shot matters more than the number.

body.html: Many beginners think that more shots mean faster progress. Fatigue often works the other way. Tired muscles make the mount less precise, the head may lift off the stock, and the same faults can repeat until they set in.

For the first lessons a session is often one or two boxes of cartridges (usually 25 in a box), as your coach suggests. As technique and strength grow, you can shoot more, step by step. Your coach sets the number for your age, fitness and the weight of your gun and cartridges.

Recoil, the push of the gun into your shoulder, adds up over a session. If your shoulder or cheek starts to hurt, you may begin to flinch: the body jerks just before the shot. Three things help: a gun that fits you, a vest with a shoulder pad and lighter cartridges. Your coach may suggest a lighter load for the first months: a cartridge with less shot (the small pellets) in it, which pushes less into your shoulder. More in Recoil, shoulder and neck and Gun fit basics.

How often you train usually matters more than how much you shoot in one go. Many coaches find that a short session weekly or twice a month does more than a long one a few times a year. With regular sessions the movement settles. After a long break the mount and swing often feel less sure, and it can take a few sessions to get your timing back.
Between sessions you can keep the movement fresh with dry practice of the mount, but only where the law allows and with an unloaded gun that you have checked. How: Dry practice of the mount.

Take breaks. Rest a few minutes between series, drink water and talk to your coach about what is happening. When accuracy drops because you are tired, it is usually better to stop after a few good targets than to keep going.
Each target costs money. A training plan helps you spend it on progress rather than on shots without a purpose. More ways to save: How to save money.

key_points.html: Fatigue often spoils technique and repeats faults
For a beginner, a session is often one or two boxes of cartridges (usually 25 in a box), as the coach suggests
Recoil adds up: a gun that fits, a shoulder pad and cartridges with less shot (a lighter load)
Regular sessions, weekly or twice a month, often beat a lot of shooting rarely
Rest between series and stop before you are really tired

did_you_know.html: Many experienced shooters train in shorter series with full focus rather than in long sessions without a break.

quiz.q: Why can a lot of shots in one go hold a beginner back?

options.text: Fatigue spoils technique and repeats faults
The traps overheat and throw worse targets
The barrels wear out after fifty shots

quiz.explain: Tired muscles mount the gun less precisely, and the same faults repeat.

quiz.q: Which plan usually gives more progress?

options.text: A long session a few times a year
A session weekly or twice a month

quiz.explain: With regular sessions the movement settles, and you lose less between sessions.

quiz.q: What can happen if recoil makes your shoulder hurt?

options.text: You start to shoot more steadily
You may start to flinch at the shot

quiz.explain: The body expects pain and jerks, so keep recoil under control with gun fit, a pad and cartridges with less shot.
